results.prompt: How do I install the Chainlink CRE agent skill into my code editor's AI agent?
results.answer:
I'll search for information about the Chainlink CRE agent skill and how to install it.Let me get the official Chainlink documentation for the specific installation steps.Based on the official Chainlink documentation, here's how to install the Chainlink CRE agent skill into your code editor's AI agent.

## What these skills are

Each skill teaches a compatible assistant how to help you with a specific product area (for example, Data Feeds or CCIP): suggested steps, guardrails, and references so you spend less time hunting docs and more time shipping. The CRE skill specifically is designed to enable developers to learn and use Chainlink Runtime Environment (CRE) quickly by referencing filtered CRE docs. It triggers when a user wants onboarding, CRE workflow generation (in TypeScript or Golang or other supported languages), workflow guidance, CRE CLI and/or SDK help, runtime operations advice, or capability selection.

## Prerequisites

You'll need two things: a coding environment where your AI assistant supports Agent Skills, and Node.js with npx available for the install command. Installation uses Vercel's CLI for the open skills ecosystem.

The skill works across major AI coding assistants — it can be installed and reused with AI coding assistants such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, and other tools that support agent skill workflows.

## Installation commands

**Basic (interactive) install:**

```
npx skills add smartcontractkit/chainlink-agent-skills
```

Running this command starts an interactive installer where you choose project-level or global installation. Pick project-level if you want the skills stored with the repository so collaborators get the same set from version control.

**Install globally for your user account (across all projects):**

```
npx skills add smartcontractkit/chainlink-agent-skills -g
```

To install skills for your user account across projects, add the -g flag.

**Install only the CRE skill (rather than the whole bundle):**

```
npx skills add smartcontractkit/chainlink-agent-skills --skill chainlink-cre-skill -g
```

If you only want one package from the bundle at user level, use --skill with the skill folder name.

## Using it

Once installed, you invoke the skill in your agent's chat by referencing it (skills are namespaced with a slash, e.g. the docs show examples like `/chainlink-ace-skill`). For the CRE skill, use the corresponding `chainlink-cre-skill` and simply describe the CRE workflow, SDK, or CLI task you want help with — the agent loads the skill's guidance automatically when the task matches.

One practical note if it doesn't appear: skills live in a folder whose name matches the skill with a `SKILL.md` inside it, so make sure the path is correct and not doubly nested.

results.prompt: When I ask the Chainlink CRE skill to build a workflow, what steps does it walk through?
results.answer:
Based on the Chainlink documentation about the CRE agent skill and the standard CRE development workflow, here's what it walks you through.

## What the CRE skill covers

The `/chainlink-cre-skill` is a documentation assistant for the Chainlink Runtime Environment. This skill covers the Chainlink Runtime Environment (CRE). It can: Install and use the CRE CLI. Create new CRE projects in Go or TypeScript. Build workflows with CRON, HTTP, or EVM log triggers, including multi-handler projects with more than one entry point. Use EVM read and write, HTTP, and confidential HTTP capabilities. Develop smart contracts that receive and verify CRE reports. Simulate workflows before deployment and write unit tests. Deploy workflows and set up monitoring.

Under the hood, the skill uses a four-step runtime pattern with 10 topic-specific reference files to route queries efficiently.

## The steps it walks through to build a workflow

The skill follows the CRE's core development loop, which progresses roughly as follows:

**1. Set up the CRE CLI and account.** You can start building and simulating CRE workflows immediately, without any approval: Create an account at app.chain.link/cre/discover to access the platform.

**2. Initialize a new project.** In this first part, you'll go from an empty directory to a fully initialized CRE project and simulate your first, minimal workflow. Concretely, this means you initialize a new project using cre init. Explore the generated project structure and workflow code. Configure your workflow for simulation. Run your first local simulation with cre workflow simulate.

**3. Choose a trigger and write the workflow logic.** Using the SDK, you build the workflow around a trigger (CRON, HTTP, or EVM log) and one or more handlers. Using the CRE SDK (available in Go and TypeScript), you build Workflows. These workflows can orchestrate HTTP APIs, smart contracts, and offchain computation.

**4. Add capabilities (offchain/onchain data).** You extend the workflow to fetch external data and read/write on chain — for example, modify your workflow to fetch data from an external API using the http.Client.

**5. Simulate locally before deploying.** Simulation compiles your workflows into WebAssembly (WASM) and runs them on your machine—but makes real calls to live APIs and public EVM blockchains. This gives you confidence your workflow will work as expected when deployed to a DON.

**6. Build and deploy to the registry.** When you're ready, this command compiles your workflow, uploads the artifacts to the CRE Storage Service, and submits a registration transaction to the registry. As the docs describe it, when you deploy a workflow, you take your locally tested code and register it with the onchain Workflow Registry contract. This makes your workflow "live" so it can activate and respond to triggers across a Decentralized Oracle Network (DON).

**7. Set up monitoring** of the deployed workflow's execution and performance.

## How execution actually runs

It's also worth noting the architecture the skill is helping you target: each workflow is orchestrated by a Workflow DON (Decentralized Oracle Network) that monitors for triggers and coordinates execution. The workflow can then invoke specialized Capability DONs—for example, one that fetches offchain data or one that writes to a chain. During execution, each node in a DON performs the requested task independently. Their results are then cryptographically verified and aggregated via a Byzantine Fault Tolerant (BFT) consensus protocol.

One practical tip: the skills are designed to be composable, so you can name more than one skill in the same message (for example /chainlink-data-feeds-skill and /chainlink-ccip-skill) when your task spans products so both sets of guardrails apply in one answer.

results.prompt: I'm new to this. When building a Chainlink CRE workflow with an AI assistant, why would I load a single page instead of the whole SDK docs, and how do I grab a single page?
results.answer:
Great question — this is a really practical thing to get right when you're pairing an AI assistant with CRE development. I wasn't able to pull the exact wording from the Chainlink docs (I hit the search tool's rate limit mid-research), so let me explain the reasoning and the general mechanics, and point you to where to confirm the specifics.

## Why load a single page instead of the whole SDK docs

It comes down to how AI assistants "read" documentation. Everything you give the model has to fit inside its **context window** — a finite budget of tokens it can hold at once. The full CRE SDK docs are large, and stuffing all of it in causes a few problems:

- **You can overflow the context window.** If the docs are bigger than the budget, the tool has to truncate or drop content — and you often can't control *what* gets cut, so critical details may silently disappear.
- **Relevance gets diluted ("needle in a haystack").** Even when everything fits, models answer more accurately when the relevant material is a large fraction of what they're looking at. Bury the one page you need inside hundreds of unrelated pages, and the assistant is more likely to grab the wrong API, mix up versions, or hallucinate.
- **Cost and speed.** More tokens = more money and slower responses, for information you probably don't need for the task at hand.
- **Focus.** If you're writing, say, an HTTP-triggered workflow, the assistant does best with the *specific* page describing that trigger/capability, not the entire reference tree.

So the rule of thumb: **give the assistant the narrowest slice of docs that fully covers your current task.** Grab the specific page for the capability, trigger, or SDK function you're using. Add more pages only when the task actually spans them.

## How to grab a single page

The Chainlink docs (docs.chain.link) are built to be AI-friendly, and there are a couple of common ways to pull one page cleanly:

1. **Use the page's "Copy page" / copy-as-Markdown action.** Most modern doc sites — Chainlink's included — put a button near the top of each page that copies the page as clean Markdown, which is exactly what you want to paste into an assistant. Look for a "Copy" or "Copy page" control on the CRE doc page you're viewing.

2. **Fetch the raw Markdown version of the URL.** Chainlink's docs serve Markdown-fidelity routes, so you can often get the plain-text/Markdown form of a page rather than the rendered HTML (which is full of nav and styling noise the model doesn't need). This is the version to hand to the AI.

3. **Point the assistant at the single URL** if your tool supports fetching, e.g. a specific reference page like:
   - `https://docs.chain.link/cre/reference/sdk/core-ts` (SDK Reference: Core)
   - `https://docs.chain.link/cre/key-terms` (Key Terms and Concepts)

   …rather than the CRE landing page or the whole reference section.

A quick practical workflow: open the exact CRE page you need → copy it as Markdown (or grab its `.md`/raw form) → paste it into your AI assistant's context → then ask your question. Repeat per page as your task grows.

---

**One honest caveat:** I couldn't fully verify the exact button label and raw-Markdown URL convention on the live Chainlink CRE docs before answering. I'd suggest opening any CRE page (like the SDK Core reference linked above) and looking for the copy/Markdown option near the title to confirm the precise mechanism. If you tell me which capability or workflow you're building, I can suggest exactly which page(s) to load.

Would you like me to look up the specific "build with AI assistants" guidance page in the CRE docs once the search tool frees up?
